> I reviewed the three analyses in `dataset-overview.qmd` against their R
> scripts (`analysis-microbiome-arm.R`, `analysis-genes-ring.R`,
> `analysis-cst-genes.R`) — and rather than just giving opinions, I **reran
> every part I would have done differently**. Every number below comes from
> `group_project/review-checks.R`, which you can run yourself (about 5
> minutes; see *How to check this page yourself* at the end).
>
> **The short answer: the three analyses are sound and I would keep almost
> all of them.** The workshop rules were followed (raw counts into DESeq2,
> column order checked, groups defined from the metadata and never from the
> table being tested), and the write-up is unusually honest about its own
> limitations. I would make **six changes**, listed here from most to least
> important. Three of them change numbers you would report.

| # | Change | What it affects | Effort |
|---|--------|-----------------|--------|
| 1 | Shrink log2FCs with `lfcShrink()` before ranking or plotting them | Which species/genes top the bar charts (fig5, fig8) — 1 of 8 top species survives | ~2 lines per chart |
| 2 | Report the unadjusted model next to the adjusted one | Q1 and Q2 headline counts (27 vs 2 species; 66 vs 165 genes) | 1 extra model each |
| 3 | Show the pill-vs-injectable contrast instead of inferring it | Defends the "route" grouping with one number (4 genes) | 1 `results()` call |
| 4 | Replace "counting significant genes" with nested LRTs | Q3's headline (162 vs 70 genes — confirms their conclusion, properly) | ~10 lines |
| 5 | Add a `betadisper()` check after every PERMANOVA | Defends the R²/p interpretations — **I ran them all; they pass** | 2 lines per test |
| 6 | Three small fixes | Species DESeq2 design, permutation count, filters | 1 line each |

## What the group already got right

Keep all of this — I would not change it:

- **Column order checked against metadata rows** before every test (with
  `stopifnot`, even though the helper already reorders — belt and braces).
- **Raw counts into DESeq2**, VST used only for plots, never for tests.
- **Groupings always from the metadata** (`arm`, `route`, and community types
  from the *species* table when testing the *gene* table — the rule kept
  precisely).
- **Adjusting for batch, BV and STI** in the gene models — the batch/armed
  balance was already checked in `01-qc.qmd`.
- **Honest caveats**: the compositional warnings, the BPIFA1–BV tangle, the
  cross-sectional "association not causation" note, and the split verdict in
  question 3 instead of forcing one story.
- **Check-yourself sections** with concrete numbers to catch mistakes.

## 1. Shrink the log2 fold changes before ranking or plotting them

**The problem.** DESeq2's first estimate of a log2FC for a feature with almost
no reads can be enormous, because a handful of reads is "infinitely" more
than zero. The bar charts (fig5, fig8) pick their bars by *largest |log2FC|
among significant hits* — which is exactly how you find the least trustworthy
estimates. Look at baseMean (the average count per sample) in the species
chart: the #1 bar, *Atopobium minutum* at **+28.29**, sits on an average of
**18 reads across 93 samples**.

**The fix.** `lfcShrink()` pulls noisy, low-count estimates toward zero while
leaving well-supported ones alone. Two lines:

```r
shr <- lfcShrink(dds, contrast = c("route", "local", "systemic"),
                 type = "normal")   # or contrast = c("arm", "ring", "pill")
plot with shr$log2FoldChange instead of res$log2FoldChange
```

**What it changes (I reran it).** For the species chart, only **1 of the top
8** bars survives in the top 8 after shrinkage:

| Their top 8 (by raw log2FC) | raw LFC | shrunk LFC | baseMean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| *Atopobium minutum* | +28.29 | **−0.80** | 18 |
| *Slackia exigua* | +24.90 | **−1.48** | 2.8 |
| *Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum* | −21.57 | −2.88 | 3.2 |
| *Fenollaria massiliensis* | +15.03 | +2.88 | 246 |
| *Mobiluncus curtisii* | +11.70 | +2.49 | 305 |
| ... | | | |

Note the *sign flips*: the +28 "enriched in ring" bar is, after shrinkage,
consistent with roughly no difference. The shrinkage-based top 8 is
*Peptoniphilus lacrimalis* (+4.6), *Dialister* (+4.3), *Prevotella timonensis*
(+4.2, baseMean 6,407), *Sneathia amnii* (+4.0) — the same BV-anaerobe story,
but now carried by species with real counts. The gene chart changes too (only
**2 of 8** survive): HSD17B13 (baseMean 8.5) and EPGN (19.7) drop out; CHGA,
KDR, PLXNA4, PTGS2, CEACAM7, UPK3B come in — which is *closer* to the prose
tables, which sensibly ranked by p-value instead.

**What it does NOT change:** the *significance* lists (the 27 species, 66
genes, etc. — padj is computed before shrinkage) or any conclusion. It changes
which features the pictures point at.

To read more: the
[DESeq2 vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html),
section "Log fold change shrinkage", and the
[`lfcShrink` reference page](https://rdrr.io/bioc/DESeq2/man/lfcShrink.html).

## 2. Report the unadjusted model next to the adjusted one

**The problem.** Both main DESeq2 models adjust for `bv` (and the gene model
for `any_sti`). The write-up treats this as free protection, but it answers a
narrower question than the headline one — and whether that matters depends on
something the document itself points out: BV may sit **on the pathway**, not
beside it.

```
confounder (adjust for it):        mediator (adjusting hides real signal):

   bv ───> tissue                      ring ──> BV-like state ──> tissue
    \                                    (BV is a consequence of the
     \                                     ring, not a rival explanation)
      arm
```

If the ring pushes the microbiome BV-ward and the BV-like tissue then changes
gene expression, then adjusting for `bv` **removes part of the ring's effect
you actually want to measure**. If instead BV is unrelated to method, the
adjustment is pure gain. Cross-sectional data can't tell you which diagram
you're in — so run both models and report both numbers. That is not
indecisive; it's two honest answers to two different questions.

**What I found when I ran both (Q2, genes, local vs systemic):**

| Design | Significant genes |
|---|---:|
| ~ batch + route (unadjusted) | **165** |
| ~ batch + bv + sti + route (their model) | **66** |

So about 100 genes' worth of route-associated signal overlaps with the
BV/STI state. Their BPIFA1 caution, stated in prose, is really a
100-gene phenomenon — worth a number in the report.

**The surprise (Q1, species, ring vs pill) goes the other way:**

| Design | Significant species |
|---|---:|
| ~ batch + arm (unadjusted) | **2** |
| ~ batch + bv + arm (their model) | **27** |

Adjusting *increased* the hits, because `bv` is essentially a summary of the
species table: putting it in the model soaks up the dominant microbiome
variation and makes small arm differences measurable. Their adjusted choice
was the right headline — but the unadjusted count (2!) is also worth stating,
because it shows how completely BV dominates the raw species-level variation.
I would report both, and say plainly: *unadjusted answers "does arm associate
with species profiles at all" (barely); adjusted answers "beyond the BV-like
state, does arm associate with any species" (27).*

## 3. Defend the "route" grouping with the contrast that tests it

The route analysis collapses pill + injectable into one "systemic" block. The
write-up defends this indirectly, via a consistency check (11 genes shared
between two ring contrasts, all agreeing in direction). There is a much more
direct test, and it's one `results()` call on a model they already fitted:
**contrast pill directly against injectable**. If the two "systemic" arms
differ from each other all over the genome, the collapse is hiding something.

I ran it (full covariate design, genes and species):

| Contrast | Significant genes | Significant species |
|---|---:|---:|
| ring vs pill | 60 | 27 |
| ring vs injectable | 87 | 14 |
| **pill vs injectable** | **4** | **6** |

The two systemic arms are nearly interchangeable (4 genes of 14,226), while
the ring differs from both — so the collapse is well justified, and this
triangle is the number that shows it. I'd put it in place of (or alongside)
the overlap-of-11 consistency check, which is a weaker and less readable
argument.

## 4. Question 3: compare groupings with nested tests, not gene counts

The document's caveat is exactly right — "the two comparisons are not formal
statistical tests of each other" — but then leaves the 93-vs-49 comparison as
the headline. There are two clean ways to test it properly, and I ran both:

**Per-gene, the right way: nested LRTs.** Fit the gene model with *both*
groupings, then ask (likelihood-ratio test, gene by gene) whether each
grouping adds anything the other hasn't already explained:

```r
# does community type add anything beyond arm, gene by gene?
DESeq(dds, test = "LRT",
      full    = ~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + arm + ctype,
      reduced = ~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + arm)
# ...and the mirror image for arm beyond ctype
```

| LRT (all adjusted for batch, bv, STI) | Significant genes |
|---|---:|
| community type **beyond** arm | **162** |
| arm **beyond** community type | **70** |

This is the same asymmetry their heuristic found (93 vs 49), but now it is an
actual test — **and their conclusion stands: the community type is the
stronger pointer to host genes.** Note 162 is bigger than their 93 because it
is a different question ("beyond arm", not "with arm ignored").

**Genome-wide, the right way: marginal PERMANOVA.** Their `perm_full`
(euc ~ type + arm, R² = 0.054, p = 0.13) is a *sequential* test — with
adonis2's default, the second term is only tested for what it adds after the
first, so the result depends on the order. Setting `by = "margin"` tests each
term as if entered last, which is the fair comparison:

```r
adonis2(euc ~ ctype + arm, data = meta, permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

My run: arm R² = 0.033 (p ≈ 0.08), ctype R² = 0.021 (p ≈ 0.4–0.5, it wobbles —
it is permutation-based). Same split verdict they honestly reported: method
edges it genome-wide, type wins per-gene. I'd just report it from the
marginal version and say why.

**If this were a paper, not a workshop**, I'd also consider replacing the
Ward clustering with [Dirichlet-multinomial
mixtures](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0030126) — the standard
generative model for community state types — and I'd cross-check the DESeq2
species calls with a compositional-aware method such as
[ANCOM-BC](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17041-7). For the
workshop, their choices are fine, and the planned k = 2 robustness rerun is
the right next check.

## 5. Add a dispersion check after every PERMANOVA

**The problem.** PERMANOVA (adonis2) asks "do groups sit in different places".
A significant result can also arise when groups are equally placed but **one
is more spread out** than another. The fix is the companion test
[`betadisper()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/vegan/man/betadisper.html): it checks
whether the groups' *spread* (dispersion) is equal. If dispersion differs,
PERMANOVA's p-value is ambiguous and you must not lean on it.

This matters doubly here, because the write-up itself noticed a dispersion
effect ("the diverse type just spreads wider" in fig9) — noticed, but never
tested.

**Good news: I ran all five checks, and every one passes:**

| PERMANOVA distance | Grouping | Dispersion p | Verdict |
|---|---|---:|---|
| microbiome Bray–Curtis | arm | 0.78 | equal spread ✓ |
| microbiome Bray–Curtis | bv | 0.71 | equal spread ✓ |
| gene expression (VST top 2000) | community type | 0.12 | equal spread ✓ |
| gene expression | route | 0.67 | equal spread ✓ |
| gene expression | arm | 0.92 | equal spread ✓ |

So their R² and p-value interpretations all stand — but in a report or a
presentation, "PERMANOVA is significant (or not) and betadisper shows the
groups are equally spread, so the test is interpretable" is the sentence that
makes it defensible. Two lines per test:

```r
bd <- betadisper(my_dist, meta$arm)
permutest(bd, permutations = 999)   # p > 0.05: dispersion is fine
```

## 6. Three small ones

1. **Add `any_sti` to the species DESeq2 design** (Q1). The PERMANOVA adjusts
   for arm + bv + any_sti + batch, but the species DESeq2 uses
   `~ rnaseq_batch + bv + arm` — the STI adjustment is in one test and not the
   other. An STI could shift specific vaginal taxa; the two models should
   agree on what they adjust for.

2. **The gene filter is a no-op — either drop the pretence or use a real one.**
   `rowSums(genes) >= 10` keeps **all 14,226** genes (even "≥ 10 reads in ≥ 5
   samples" keeps all 14,226). Only a presence-based rule trims anything
   (14,224 genes at ≥ 10 reads in ≥ 9 samples). For the **species** table it
   does matter: presence in ≥ 5 samples would keep **72** of 220, versus
   their 110 — a prevalence filter is the more standard choice and would
   shrink the multiple-testing burden. Either way, don't describe a filter
   that filters nothing.

3. **When a permutation p-value is borderline, don't report "≈ 0.1".**
   The arm-alone PERMANOVA (R² = 0.03, p "≈ 0.1, wobbles") is the one result
   nearest a decision boundary, and 999 permutations is coarse there. Use
   9,999 permutations and `set.seed()` so the number is stable and
   reportable to three decimals. (I would *not* change the conclusion — arm
   alone remains weakly-at-best significant either way.)

## Question-by-question summary

| Question | Keep | I would change |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Microbiome by arm | Everything, incl. the bv-adjusted DESeq2 as headline | Shrink LFCs before fig5; report the unadjusted count (2 vs 27) with a sentence on why they differ; add `any_sti` to the design; 9,999-perm PERMANOVA |
| 2. Ring vs systemic genes | Route framing, covariate adjustment, direction-consistency logic | Shrink LFCs before fig8; report unadjusted 165 alongside adjusted 66 and say the difference is the BV/STI pathway, not noise; defend the collapse with the pill-vs-injectable contrast (4 genes) |
| 3. Type vs method | Ward k = 3 clustering, LRT-with-adjustment idea, the two-view (gene-counts + R²) framing | Make the comparison formal: nested LRTs (162 vs 70 — same conclusion) and `adonis2(by = "margin")`; run betadisper (passes) |

## How to check this page yourself

Every number in this review comes from one script:

```
Rscript group_project/review-checks.R
```

Compare its printed output with the numbers above. The ones that would catch
me being wrong:

- Section 1: gene filter keeps **14,226 of 14,226** (a no-op); species
  presence-filter keeps **72**.
- Section 2: species sig counts **27** (matches their report) and top-8
  raw-vs-shrunk overlap **1 of 8**.
- Section 3: genes **66** (matches), overlap **2 of 8**.
- Section 4: unadjusted models **2** (species) and **165** (genes) vs their
  adjusted **27** and **66**.
- Section 5: pill vs injectable **4** genes; ring contrasts **60 / 87**
  (match their report).
- Section 6: nested LRTs **162** vs **70**; marginal PERMANOVA R² 0.021 /
  0.033.
- Section 7: all five betadisper p-values > 0.05 (they will wobble in the last
  decimal — permutation tests do that).

## Choices made

- **Reviewed by rerunning, not re-reading**: I repeated every analysis I
  criticised, on the same data with the same rules — alternative rejected:
  reviewing the code only, without checking the criticisms against the data.
- **Shrinkage method `type = "normal"`** (works with `contrast`) —
  alternatives not chosen: `apeglm` or `ashr` (need coefficient indices, and
  ashr needs an extra package; both fine, slightly more setup).
- **Report both adjusted and unadjusted models rather than pick one** —
  alternative rejected: treating the bv-adjusted model as simply "better",
  which hides the ~100-gene question the mediator diagram raises.
- **Route-collapse checked with the direct pill-vs-injectable contrast** —
  alternative not chosen: a formal LRT of `arm` vs `route` designs (nearly
  equivalent, harder to explain).
- **Q3 compared with nested LRTs and marginal PERMANOVA** — alternative
  rejected: keeping the significant-gene-count heuristic as the headline
  (their own caveat already says why not).
- **All five dispersion checks run at 999 permutations** — alternative not
  chosen: skipping them because the PERMANOVAs looked fine (that would be
  assuming the conclusion).
- **Numbers quoted from my runs rounded to the precision that survives
  reruns** (permutation p-values reported as approximate) — alternative
  rejected: quoting exact p-values that would not reproduce.
- **Kept their k = 3 Ward clustering for all comparisons** so my numbers are
  comparable to theirs — alternative not chosen: rerunning everything at
  k = 2 as well (worth doing later; their document already suggests it).
- **Review shipped as static tables plus a reproducible script** —
  alternative rejected: live code chunks in this document (they would take
  ~5 minutes every render).
- **Plain default Quarto styling** — alternative rejected: copying the
  custom CSS of `dataset-overview.html` (cosmetic; not worth the extra file).
